newsitem.title: UK: Short sterling seen undervalued into 1998 -traders.
newsitem.headline: Short sterling seen undervalued into 1998 -traders.

text.p: Short sterling futures traded on LIFFE are pricing in too negative a view of British interest rates, traders said on Thursday.

Short sterling futures have been hit over the past months by concerns that interest rates will have to rise to curb inflationary pressures. The June contract has fallen from a high of 93.66 in mid-March to its current 93.30.
They are also vulnerable to the weakness in U.S. and German debt markets.

"Short sterling is being dragged down by losses in the Bunds, but you can see by the way a 30 tick drop in Bunds translates to just one tick in short sterling that people don't want to sell it down," said a broker at a major British bank here. "The strip is looking cheap."

British base rates are currently at 6.0 percent, after a rise of 25 basis points in October last year. Since then, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has ignored pressure from governor of the Bank of England Eddie George to raise interest rates.
Traders said if the opposition Labour Party wins the May 1 election, they will have to raise rates almost immediately.
A trader at a U.S. bank here noted that the volumes during a falling market were light, suggesting that investors were unconvinced by the weakness.

"As soon as it dips, people buy it," the U.S. bank trader said. "Okay, rates are going to have to rise soon. But there's too much bad news priced in. Labour could put a quarter, or even a half point on rates by the end of the year, but no more."
A British bank trader said even a rate hike of 50 basis points would still mean that the September short sterling future had about 25 basis points of extra value.
The short sterling strip implies interest rates of 7.0 percent in September, 7.25 percent in December, rising to 7.75 percent in December 1998.
